To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

SEDL, a protein that is responsible for a human disease, is similar to the N-terminal regulatory domains of two proteins involved in vesicular trafficking, and that the mutations in the SEDL gene responsible for the disease are located in the interior of the protein and on a surface, respectively.

SEDL is structurally related to SNAREs despite no sequence homologous to them, and that three out of four known missense SEDL mutations responsible for a skeletal disease are likely to disrupt protein structure.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular mechanisms of the disease SEDT.
the structural and functional characterization of SEDL.
the structural characterization of the SEDL protein and its implications for SEDT.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the SEDL mutations are likely to cause the disease through disruption of protein-protein interactions.
SEDL is structurally related to the SNARE regulatory domains but is not a SNARE protein.

the structure of SEDT is consistent with a role of SEDL in protein-protein interactions, and the mutations are likely to be disease-causing by affecting the structure of the protein or its interactions with other proteins.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the structure of SEDT is similar to that of SNAREs, but the function of SEDT remains to be identified.
the SEDL structure provides insights into the molecular basis of SEDL’s function and its disease-causing mutations.
SEDL is a novel member of the SNARE family, which may be involved in protein-protein interactions and/or membrane fusion.
The main takeaway from our work is that
SEDL is a novel protein with no known homologs in prokaryotes, and that it may serve regulatory and/or adaptor roles in vesicle trafficking.
the structure of SEDT is a good model for the structure of the N-terminal domain of SNAREs, which is important in the regulation of SNARE complex formation.
the structure and function of SEDL are likely to be highly conserved in eukaryotes.
